messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 46-year-old park ranger who came to treatment after months of telling his wife he was only “stressed” and could handle it on his own. He had served in combat years earlier, and when he describes the worst event, he does so with a flat, controlled voice that slips at the edges. His unit had been moving through a dry area under aircraft overhead when the situation turned suddenly. He remembers the chopping sound above them, the abrupt blasts, the smell in the air that mixed fuel, hot dust, and something burned, and the moment he froze while another man closer to the line of fire went down. What has stayed with him is not only terror but a settled conviction that he failed a test that mattered: he did not do enough, fast enough, and something in him has been wrong ever since.

In the years after coming home, Kwame built a life that seemed to fit someone who liked the outdoors and structure. As a park ranger, he spends long stretches on trails, at entrance stations, and around campgrounds, listening for changes in weather, watching visitors, and responding to problems before they grow. But the sounds of helicopters or low aircraft passing over the park cut through him immediately. On those days he feels uncomfortable in his own body before he can think clearly about why, and sometimes, standing near a trailhead or ranger vehicle, he has the unnerving sensation that things are becoming unreal, as if he is slightly outside himself. The moment that happens, he goes on high alert. He starts tracking every sudden noise, watches visitors’ hands and movements more closely, and scans tree lines, parked cars, and open ground as if danger might emerge from anywhere.

These reactions do not feel random to him. Each time he catches himself flinching at aircraft noise or feeling detached, it confirms what he has come to believe about himself: that he is permanently changed for the worse and that ordinary people do not live like this. He tells himself he has to be on guard all the time because he is no longer capable of relaxing safely. The trigger is frightening not just because it startles him, but because it seems to prove that the war is still inside him, ready to take over.

His beliefs about what happened also shape how quickly he is set off now. Because he is certain that vigilance is necessary, he moves through the park already keyed up, listening for engines and loud sounds and bracing against the possibility of feeling detached. A helicopter carrying tourists over the canyon, or even aircraft he cannot yet see, can become the focus of his attention long before it is overhead. He has come to expect these moments, and that expectation seems to make them easier to trip.

Once he is in that state of alert, the memories come with unusual force. If he hears unexpected loud sounds while on patrol, he does not simply remember the combat incident in outline; the memory arrives with sharp detail, more vivid than most of the rest of his life. He can almost smell again the fuel and scorched air from that day, and he describes those moments as more real than normal memory, as if the past is pressing directly into the present. Watching other people closely for possible harm and scanning his surroundings seem to pull him back toward the same sensory fragments, as though his mind is searching the current scene for the old danger and finding the old images instead.

Those memories, in turn, deepen the conclusions he has drawn about himself. When the smell and sound come back so vividly, he is overwhelmed by guilt that he did not do more to stop what happened. He reads the intensity of the memory as evidence that he has never truly left the event and never will. To him, the fact that the past can feel this immediate means the damage is permanent.

His constant watchfulness has also begun to feed those same beliefs. At work he monitors visitors so closely that he rarely feels at ease, even on routine days, and by the time he gets home he is exhausted and irritable. He sees this exhaustion as proof that his mind cannot switch off and that being on guard is now simply who he is. On the trail, if a sudden sound makes him tense and detached, the reaction itself becomes another warning sign to him that he is not safe inside his own body.

What finally brought Kwame in was an incident in the park when a helicopter passed low during a busy afternoon and he lost his sense of the present for several seconds while speaking with a family asking for directions. He recovered quickly, but he was shaken by how unreal everything had felt and by how intensely the old smells and images rushed back afterward. He is afraid that he has become a man who will always live as if an attack is about to happen, and that his wife is right when she says he has been disappearing even while standing next to her. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is not to erase the past but to stop living as if every sound overhead means he is back there again.
